questions.question: A primary benefit of inserting a message queue between services is:
options: Forcing synchronous coupling so both sides fail together always.
Decoupling producers and consumers and absorbing bursts asynchronously.
Guaranteeing the UI paints pixels without any backend at all.
Removing the need for authentication on every public API.

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: The basic architecture of a message queue is simple. Input services, called producers/publishers, create messages, and publish them to a message queue.

questions.question: Notification systems often place a queue before SMS/email/push workers to:
options: Drop all messages silently when traffic is high.
Buffer send jobs and scale workers independently of API traffic.
Encrypt the queue by turning off TLS on purpose.
Make push notifications require a human operator to click Send.

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide

questions.question: If a queue delivers at-least-once, consumers should:
options: Assume exactly-once and double-charge users freely.
Be idempotent so retries do not corrupt state.
Crash the whole cluster on the first duplicate delivery.
Disable acknowledgements so messages never leave the queue.

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: Design locality applies to most of the system components: crawl servers, cache, queue, storage, etc. 4.

questions.question: True or false: Queues trade immediate completion for resilience and smoother load.

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide

questions.question: A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is useful when:
options: Every message succeeds on the first try forever.
Poison messages fail repeatedly and need isolation / inspection.
You want to delete monitoring because failures never happen.
Producers should block forever without any backoff.

reference.book: Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann
